content: 1. A study published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS in 2013 evaluated the effectiveness of various HIV testing strategies among African American men who have sex with men (MSM). The findings highlighted the importance of targeted interventions to increase testing uptake in this population. 2. Flavien T. and colleagues presented a community-driven intervention at the 2017 International AIDS Society Conference in Paris. This program incentivized clients of sex workers to undergo HIV testing, demonstrating the potential of community-based approaches to improve testing rates. 3. Guo Y. and colleagues, in a 2011 study published in AIDS Care, compared four sampling methods for HIV/STD surveillance among MSM in China. The research provided critical insights into optimizing surveillance and prevention strategies for this population. 4. Halkitis PN and colleagues, in a 2011 study in Annals of Behavioral Medicine, assessed the relative effectiveness of three HIV testing strategies targeting African American MSM in New York City. The study underscored the need for tailored approaches to address the unique barriers faced by this group. 5. Ifekandu C. and colleagues utilized social networking strategies to reach hard-to-access MSM populations in Lagos, Nigeria. Their findings, presented at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in Amsterdam in 2018, emphasized the role of digital platforms in expanding HIV testing services. 6. Kan M. and colleagues, in a 2018 study published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, explored social network methods for identifying HIV cases among people who inject drugs in Tajikistan. The study demonstrated the utility of leveraging social connections to enhance case-finding efforts. 7. Katz D. and colleagues, in a 2016 study in Sexually Transmitted Diseases, showed that partner services for sexually transmitted infections significantly increased HIV testing among the partners of MSM. This approach highlights the importance of partner notification in HIV prevention. 8. Lightfoot MA and colleagues, in a 2018 study in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, demonstrated the effectiveness of a social network strategy to distribute HIV self-test kits to African American and Latino MSM. This method improved access to testing in underserved communities. 9. Lillie T. and colleagues, at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in 2018, presented a performance-based incentive program in Côte d’Ivoire. This initiative increased HIV case-finding among key populations by leveraging social networks. 10. Potasin P. and colleagues, at the same conference, described a peer-driven recruitment model to enhance HIV testing coverage among transgender women in Pattaya. The program successfully expanded testing access in this high-risk group. 11. Smyrnov P. and colleagues, in a 2018 study in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, utilized risk network approaches to locate undiagnosed HIV cases in Odessa, Ukraine. This innovative method targeted individuals within high-risk social networks. 12. Carballo-Dieguez A. and colleagues, in a 2012 study in AIDS and Behavior, demonstrated that the use of rapid HIV home tests prevented HIV exposure in a high-risk sample of MSM. This study highlighted the potential of self-testing in reducing transmission. 13. Linjongrat D. and colleagues, at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in 2018, discussed the accreditation of HIV clinical services provided by key populations. This approach aimed to increase domestic financing for civil society organizations involved in the HIV response. 14. Thirumurthy H. and colleagues, in a 2016 study in The Lancet HIV, evaluated the secondary distribution of HIV self-tests by HIV-negative female sex workers and women receiving antenatal care in Kenya. The study demonstrated the effectiveness of this strategy in promoting male partner testing and safer sexual decision-making. 15. Beougher SC and colleagues, in a 2015 study in Archives of Sexual Behavior, explored the motivations for HIV testing among concordant HIV-negative and HIV-discordant gay male couples. The findings provided insights into relationship dynamics influencing testing behaviors. 16. Carballo-Dieguez A. and colleagues, in a 2012 study in Journal of Sex Research, investigated whether high-risk gay and bisexual men would use over-the-counter rapid HIV tests to screen sexual partners. The study revealed significant interest in this approach as a risk reduction strategy. 17. Chanda MM and colleagues, in a 2017 study in AIDS Patient Care and STDs, identified barriers and facilitators to HIV testing among Zambian female sex workers in transit hubs. The findings emphasized the need for targeted interventions in these high-risk settings. 18. Fields EL and colleagues, in a 2019 study in American Journal of Health Promotion, examined the use of geosocial networking apps to access young Black gay, bisexual, and other MSM at risk for HIV. The study highlighted the potential of digital tools in reaching vulnerable populations. 19. Godbole S. and colleagues, at the 9th IAS Conference on HIV Science in 2017, discussed the provision of HIV testing services at the doorstep for hard-to-reach sex workers in India. This approach significantly increased testing uptake in this hidden population. 20. Maman S. and colleagues, in a 2017 study in PLOS One, conducted a qualitative analysis of the secondary distribution of HIV self-test kits by female sex workers in Kenya. The study highlighted the acceptability and feasibility of this approach in increasing testing coverage. 21. Mitchell JW and Sullivan PS, in a 2015 study in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, examined factors associated with the willingness to use in-home rapid HIV tests to screen potential sexual partners among HIV-negative and HIV-discordant male couples in the U.S. 22. Sharma A. and colleagues, in a 2017 study in AIDS Care, assessed the willingness of MSM in the U.S. to distribute free rapid home HIV test kits and test with their social or sexual network associates. The findings supported the feasibility of this community-based approach. 23. Tobin K. and colleagues, in a 2018 study in AIDS Care, evaluated the acceptability and feasibility of a peer mentor program to train young Black MSM to promote HIV and STI home-testing within their social networks. 24. Woodward CL and colleagues, in a 2010 study in Sex Health, conducted a computer-assisted survey to assess attitudes toward HIV and STI partner notification among HIV-positive MSM. The study provided insights into the acceptability of partner notification strategies. 25. Xu H. and colleagues, at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in 2018, explored the acceptability and feasibility of promoting HIV testing to sexual partners using self-testing among HIV-positive MSM in Guangzhou, China. 26. Golden MR and colleagues, in a 2006 study in AIDS, demonstrated the effectiveness of peer referral for HIV case-finding among MSM. This approach leveraged social networks to identify undiagnosed cases. 27. Solomon SS and colleagues, in a 2017 study in PLOS Medicine, utilized respondent-driven sampling to identify HIVand HCV-infected individuals among people who inject drugs and MSM in India. The study highlighted the utility of this method in community-based settings. 28. Zulliger R. and colleagues, in a 2017 study in AIDS and Behavior, conducted a cost-utility analysis of HIV testing programs among MSM in the U.S. The findings emphasized the economic benefits of targeted testing interventions.
